title: Nitrogen compounds
overview: Understand phenylamine, azo dye formation, and the structure of amides and amino acids. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Prepare primary/secondary amines and compare their basicity.
Describe phenylamine reactions, diazotisation and azo coupling.
Explain amino-acid zwitterions, acid–base behaviour and peptide links.

definitions.definition: An ammonia derivative with one or more H atoms replaced by carbon groups.
Conversion of a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt using nitrous acid below 10 °C.
A species carrying both positive and negative charges but no overall charge.
The amide link –CONH– formed between amino acids.
Tendency to accept a proton, governed by lone-pair availability.

sections.title: Preparing amines
content: Heat a halogenoalkane with excess ethanolic NH₃ under pressure for a primary amine; reaction with a primary amine can form a secondary amine. Reduce nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni, and reduce amides with LiAlH₄. Choose routes by the required carbon skeleton.
bullets: Nitrile reduction adds/retains the nitrile carbon in the chain.

sections.title: Basicity
content: Amines accept H⁺ through the N lone pair. Alkyl groups donate electron density and usually make aliphatic amines stronger bases than NH₃. Phenylamine is weaker because its lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation.
bullets: Compare lone-pair availability in the conjugate pair.
Amides are much weaker bases because the N lone pair is delocalised into C=O.

sections.title: Phenylamine and azo chemistry
content: Phenylamine reacts with bromine water to form 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine. With NaNO₂/dilute acid below 10 °C it forms a diazonium salt, which can warm with water to phenol or couple with activated rings such as phenol in alkaline conditions to form coloured azo compounds.
bullets: Show the azo –N=N– linkage between aromatic groups.

sections.title: Amides and amino acids
content: Acyl chlorides react with NH₃/amines to form amides. Amides hydrolyse under acidic or alkaline conditions to carboxylic-acid/carboxylate products and ammonium/amine products. Amino acids exist as zwitterions near neutral pH, form cations in acid and anions in alkali, and condense through –COOH and –NH₂ to form peptide links.
bullets: Draw ionic forms with correct charges.
Peptide hydrolysis restores amino-acid functional groups.

examTips: Use structures, not only names, for amino-acid ionic forms and azo products.
When selecting an amine synthesis, track every carbon atom through the route.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Saying the phenylamine lone pair is unavailable because nitrogen has no lone pair.
Forgetting cold conditions for diazonium formation.
Drawing an amino acid with incompatible protonation states for the stated pH.

quickRecall.question: Why is phenylamine weaker than an alkylamine?
quickRecall.answer: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring and is less available to accept H⁺.

quickRecall.question: Why is diazotisation kept below 10 °C?
quickRecall.answer: Aromatic diazonium salts decompose more readily when warmed.

quickRecall.question: What forms when an amino acid is placed in acid?
quickRecall.answer: The amine is protonated, giving an overall cationic form.
